_about: Queue for the 'Yes, but' guide strand (owner-approved idea 2026-10-08; flow built, NOT started). Process: .claude/skills/yes-but-guide/SKILL.md. Every verdictHypothesis below is UNVERIFIED -- it is what we expect to find, and the facts ledger must confirm or overturn it before any drafting. If verification overturns it into a flat 'No', the article is dropped or reframed, never forced.
_why: Research 2026-10-08: the three best-clicked guides open 'Yes, ... but' (Romex 11 clicks/90d at pos 5.8, fuse box 7 at 4.8, aluminum wiring 5 at 12.9). Same-shape guides opening with a flat 'No, a standard inspection does not...' rank similarly but get 0-1 clicks: the snippet answers them. items.question: Can you put a GFCI on an ungrounded outlet?
items.verdictHypothesis: Yes -- a GFCI can replace a two-prong receptacle with no ground, but it must be labeled 'No Equipment Ground' and it does not provide a ground for surge protectors or three-prong equipment.
sourcesToVerify: NEC 406.4(D)(2) replacement-of-non-grounding-receptacle text, at a primary or official publisher copy (NFPA free-access NFPA 70, or a state-adopted copy)
CPSC or ESFI page on GFCI protection, for what a GFCI does and does not do
the site's open-ground guide, for consistency and a natural link
items.decision: 2026-10-08: covered by open-ground-mean-electrical-inspection (section "Installing GFCI Protection": No Equipment Ground label, GFCI does not create a ground; 487 impr/28d at pos 12.5) and linked from need-gfci-outlets-pass-home-inspection. A new URL would compete with it. Not written.

items.question: Can you put a new roof over old shingles?
items.verdictHypothesis: Yes, once -- the IRC allows a recover over one existing layer in many cases, but not over two layers, wet or deteriorated roofing, or where the manufacturer forbids it; buyers should know how many layers a roof has.
sourcesToVerify: IRC section on reroofing / recovering (R908.3.1 and its exceptions) at ICC's free public-access code (codes.iccsafe.org)
a shingle manufacturer's installation instruction on recovering, only if it can be read at the manufacturer's own site
PRIORITY_RULES roof_age for the replacement cost range (read at run time, never retyped)
items.decision: 2026-10-08: covered by how-to-tell-how-old-a-roof-is (roof recover, IRC limit of two applications, full tear-off). Not written.

items.question: Can you connect PEX or copper to galvanized pipe?
items.verdictHypothesis: Yes, with a listed transition fitting, but galvanized supply lines of that era corrode from the inside, so a partial repipe can leave the worst pipe in place.
sourcesToVerify: the plumbing code section on joints between different materials (IRC P2906 / IPC 605) at codes.iccsafe.org
PRIORITY_RULES galvanized_supply for era and repipe cost (read at run time)
the site's pipes guide, for consistency
item 4 sources: IRC/IPC text on dielectric or approved joints between copper and galvanized steel
items.decision: 2026-10-08: merged with item 4 (the queue anticipated it): one guide answers both joins. Only passing mentions exist (unpermitted-work, amateur-workmanship guides).

items.question: Can you mix copper and galvanized pipe?
items.verdictHypothesis: Yes, but only through a dielectric fitting or another approved method that separates the two metals; a direct joint corrodes.
sourcesToVerify: IRC/IPC text requiring dielectric or approved joints between dissimilar metals, at codes.iccsafe.org
check overlap with item 3 first: if the two answers share most of their body, merge them into one guide

items.question: Can you get home insurance with a wood stove?
items.verdictHypothesis: Yes in many cases, but your carrier may ask how and when it was installed, whether it is listed, and for an inspection; the answer varies by carrier and state.
sourcesToVerify: NFPA 211 scope and the Level 2 inspection trigger (consistent with the chimney rule in PRIORITY_RULES)
a state insurance department or NAIC consumer page on wood stoves and insurance, if one can be read
CARRIER RULE: never name an insurer; never 'most/many carriers will ...' -- write 'your carrier may' and how to get a written answer
items.note: Owner said "publish now" on 2026-10-08, overriding the one-a-day pace convention (Claude's, not an owner rule). No honest inbound anchor found; tier 3 demand, so no targetKeywords entry.

items.question: Can you insulate over knob-and-tube wiring?
items.verdictHypothesis: Generally no -- the NEC does not allow knob-and-tube in hollow spaces filled with insulation -- but some jurisdictions allow it after an electrician's evaluation; check the local rule.
sourcesToVerify: NEC 394.12 uses-not-permitted text at a primary or official copy
at least one state or city rule that permits insulation after inspection, read at that jurisdiction's own site -- if none can be verified, the 'but' is cut and this item is dropped
consistency with the site's knob-and-tube guides
items.decision: 2026-10-08: covered by splice-romex-knob-tube-wiring (NEC prohibits insulation around active K&T) -- the site's best page -- and what-is-knob-and-tube-wiring. Not written.

items.question: Can you make the seller pay for an unpermitted deck you find after closing?
items.addedFrom: Owner-approved idea from an outside research report (2026-10-08); the report's other gaps were already covered.
items.verdictHypothesis: Sometimes -- if the seller knew and failed to disclose it where state law requires disclosure, a buyer may have a claim, but an as-is sale, a disclosed deck or a public permit record the buyer could have checked can weaken it; it varies by state, and a real-estate attorney decides.
sourcesToVerify: COVERAGE FIRST: compare against legalize-unpermitted-deck (121 impr/90d, pos 6.2), find-unpermitted-work-before-buying, unpermitted-work-behind-the-wall and happens-if-seller-didn-t-disclose-past-insurance-claim; if the answer would mostly repeat them, drop this item
at least two state seller-disclosure statutes or official disclosure forms that ask about unpermitted work or additions, read at the state's own site
no legal-advice framing: state what the law says and when to ask an attorney; never 'you can sue'

items.question: Can homeowners insurance cancel your policy after you buy a house because of the roof?
items.addedFrom: Owner question 2026-10-10, with an outside brief (treated as unverified data).
items.verdictHypothesis: Sometimes, mainly in the first weeks; after that state law narrows cancellation, and roof age is handled at renewal with notice.
sourcesToVerify: Texas Insurance Code 551.104/551.105/551.002
Florida Statutes 627.4133 and 627.7011(5)
12 CFR 1024.37 force-placed insurance
a regulator definition of a binder
items.decision: 2026-10-10: coverage check -- home-insurance-aerial-photos-roof (#312) covers aerial-image NONRENEWALS and regulator complaints; prove-roof-age-for-insurance (#307) covers documenting roof age. Neither answers when an insurer may CANCEL mid-term after closing. New page keeps to cancellation timing, buyer rights and the mortgage consequence, and links #312/#307 rather than repeating them. Demand tier 3 (capture 2026-10-10-demand-homeowners-insurance-cancel-after-buying-*). Cluster corrected to roofing-exterior: guideTopic matches 'roof' before 'insurance', the same cluster as its roof-insurance siblings.
